framework: LangChain; MetaGPT; AutoGen; CAMEL; CrewAI; LangGraph
failure_observed: A single atomic false claim seeded into one agent is reused through message dependencies until most agents adopt it and the system converges on a false consensus.
locus_detail: Benign condition: tracer seed prefixed to the system-level directive of the entry, hub or leaf agent; attack condition: application-level injected inter-agent message aimed at high-influence nodes (aggregator, summarizer, decision-maker)
evaluation: Six frameworks in chain, mesh and star topologies; QUANT (UCI), RIGID (MATH/AMC) and MMLU retrieval tasks, 20 instances each; infection coverage S(t), ASR, BICR, Safe Completion, token and latency cost; GPT-4o-mini for decomposition and verification; baselines Reflection, AGrail, CFG
limitation: Binary adoption variable may miss partial internalization; the injection study is a controlled probe, not a full model of adaptive adversaries.
evidence_note: trigger: endogenous seed 'prefixing a fixed instruction to that agent's system-level directive' (App. B) vs 'application-level message injection' attacks (§VII-A); trigger_evidence_level: same six frameworks, but paper separates system-level seed from application-layer injection and attack targets high-influence nodes (§V), so not same role-and-interface; locus: tracer seed in entry agent's system-level instructions (§IV-A), injected messages (§V); spread: S(t) = fraction of agents adopting seed per message step, 'five reach 100% final infection' (Fig. 4, §III); defense_family: lineage graph of atomic claims, screen/block/rollback of messages on message path (§VI-B to VI-E); defense_evaluated_against: Table V reports BICR only under Baseline, Compliance and Security FUD attack settings; abstract claims endogenous suppression too but no clean-seed defense table found in sections read
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending. Abstract says the governance layer suppresses endogenous and exogenous amplification; experiments in the sections read evaluate it only under attack settings. trigger_evidence_level is a judgment call (same frameworks, different interface and target).

failure_observed: Adversarial content accepted at one inter-agent boundary is forwarded as trusted input, enabling prompt injection, consensus poisoning, plan hijacking and Sybil substitution that corrupt the final output.
locus_detail: Benign: TRAIL production traces of GAIA CodeAgent->ToolCallingAgent and SWE-Bench CodeAgent; attacks on a custom ten-agent five-layer pipeline: retrieval content into Researcher (A1), orchestrator result aggregation (A2), Planner completion signal (A3), routing slot of parallel agents (A4)
evaluation: 147 annotated TRAIL traces (GAIA, SWE-Bench Lite; 836 error instances); 20 tasks x 3 payload variants x 4 attacks x 3 models = 1,080 attack runs plus 90 clean runs; ASR, task accuracy, recovery rate, hop count; GPT-5-mini, Claude Sonnet 4.5, Kimi K2.5
limitation: Reviewer: one custom pipeline only; benign evidence comes from other systems (TRAIL traces); no defense implemented or tested.
evidence_note: trigger: benign failures from '147 annotated traces from the TRAIL benchmark' (§III) plus controlled attacks A1-A4 (§IV); trigger_evidence_level: benign traces are GAIA two-tier and SWE-Bench single CodeAgent pipelines, attacks run on a different ten-agent pipeline, mapped to the same boundary classes (§III, §IV); locus: A1 'poisoned source' retrieved content (Fig. 1), A2/A3 orchestrator accepts sub-agent result or planner signal (§III-B, C), A4 Sybil at routing position (§III-D); spread: 'payloads traverse 4-6 hops across the full execution-to-output path' (Fig. 6d, §IV-A)
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending.

framework: ChatDev; MetaGPT; HyperAgent; AppWorld; AG2 (MathChat); Magentic-One; OpenManus
failure_observed: MAS fail through system design flaws (disobeying task or role specs, repetition, termination), inter-agent misalignment (withholding, ignoring input, derailment) and weak task verification.
locus_detail: FC1 agent role and task specifications (e.g., ChatDev CPO ends without CEO), FC2 agent-to-agent conversation (e.g., Phone Agent withholds API format from Supervisor), FC3 verifier agents
evaluation: 1,642 traces from 7 MAS on ProgramDev, SWE-Bench Lite, AppWorld Test-C, GSM-Plus, GAIA, OlympiadBench, MMLU; failure-mode prevalence; GPT-4/4o, Claude 3.7 Sonnet, Qwen2.5-Coder-32B, CodeLlama-7B; LLM annotator (o1) kappa 0.77 vs humans; case-study interventions on AG2 and ChatDev
limitation: Authors do not claim MAST covers every failure pattern; interventions give only modest gains and task completion stays low.
evidence_note: trigger: failures are 'instances where the MAS does not achieve its intended task objectives' in normal runs, no adversary (§1, §3); trigger_evidence_level: only benign runs collected (Table 1); locus: FC1 'originate from system design decisions, and poor or ambiguous prompt specifications', FC2 'breakdown in critical information flow' between agents (§4); defense_family: improved prompts, verifier role, cyclic topology with CTO/Verifier termination (App. H.1, H.2); defense_evaluated_against: tested on GSM-Plus, ProgramDev-v0, HumanEval normal runs (Table 5)

framework: MetaGPT; Self-collab; Camel; SPP; MAD; AgentVerse
failure_observed: A faulty agent that introduces errors into its outputs lowers overall task performance; linear and flat structures degrade more than hierarchical ones.
locus_detail: The designated faulty agent of each system (Table 1: e.g., Code Engineer in MetaGPT, Coder in Self-collab, Assistant in Camel, Debater in MAD, Solver in AgentVerse): its profile (AutoTransform) or its outgoing messages (AutoInject)
evaluation: HumanEval, CIAR, CommonMT, FairEval; Pass@1, accuracy, BLEURT-style scores; GPT-3.5 and GPT-4o; 6 systems in linear, flat, hierarchical structures with 2-5 agents; error rates Pm and Pe, syntactic vs semantic errors
limitation: Only GPT-3.5/GPT-4o backbones and four text-only benchmarks; structure effects entangled with each system's own prompts.
evidence_note: trigger: AutoTransform rewrites profile 'to transform the original agent to a vicious agent' that deliberately inserts errors (App. C.3), adversarial; AutoInject rewrites messages to contain errors with no instruction to the agent (App. C.4), benign by codebook rule; trigger_evidence_level: both methods act on the same 'Faulty Agent' per system (Table 1), profile vs message interface, judged same role; locus: profile of faulty agent (Fig. 2c) and its messages intercepted (Fig. 2d); defense_family: Challenger adds message-checking to each agent's profile, Inspector 'an additional agent that intercepts all messages... checks for errors, and corrects them' (§5); defense_evaluated_against: tested 'with errors introduced by AutoInject or AutoTransform' (§5, Fig. 3)
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending. direct-both is a judgment: AutoTransform (instructed vicious profile) and AutoInject (message error injection) hit the same 'Faulty Agent' role through two interfaces.

failure_observed: Byzantine (faulty) agents in a 7-node network send wrong answers that can pull honest agents and the consensus away from the correct answer.
locus_detail: Byzantine nodes placed randomly or at critical positions (star center, tree root, high-centrality nodes), implemented as weaker LLMs
evaluation: GSM8K, XSTest, CommonsenseQA (10 curated questions each); IAA, FAA, round-level accuracy, BFTI; GPT-4o-mini vs GPT-3.5-turbo (PCP), LLaMA3.1-8B vs LLaMA3-8B (HCP); six topologies (complete, star, tree, chain, random, layered), 6 of 7 nodes Byzantine; 15-node extension in appendix
limitation: Reviewer: faults simulated only by weaker models on 10 curated questions per task; no instructed malicious agents despite the 'malicious' label.
evidence_note: trigger: 'strong-weak model pairs to simulate natural performance variability'; Byzantine agents 'use LLaMA3-8B-Instruct' or GPT-3.5-turbo (Experimental results), no instruction to deceive, so benign despite 'malicious' label; trigger_evidence_level: only weak-model faults; locus: Byzantine agent nodes, placement strategies (App. A.3); defense_family: 'confidence-guided Byzantine consensus protocol ... assigning higher transmission weights to more credible agents' (Methods); defense_evaluated_against: evaluated under 85.7% weak-model Byzantine nodes (Table 2)
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending. Paper calls Byzantine agents 'malicious' but implements them as weaker LLMs; coded benign-bug per codebook.

failure_observed: A malicious prompt in external content hijacks one agent and self-replicates through inter-agent messages, enabling data theft, scams, malware spread and content manipulation.
locus_detail: First tool-specific agent (email/PDF/web reader) reading infected content, then agent-to-agent messages under global or local messaging; in society simulation one citizen's system instructions overridden, spread via pairwise dialogue and memory importance scoring
evaluation: 120 user instructions x 3 tool types (360 pairs) plus synthetic CSV for data theft; ASR; GPT-4o and GPT-3.5 Turbo; application pipelines with growing agent counts, LLM town with 10-50 agents; 6 prompt defenses with/without LLM Tagging
limitation: Only GPT-family models; basic architectures; handcrafted attacks, algorithmic prompts may bypass LLM Tagging.
evidence_note: trigger: 'A malicious actor injects a single infectious prompt into external content' (§3); trigger_evidence_level: no benign condition; locus: infected document read by first agent then 'propagates it to the next agent' (§3.2, Fig. 2), direct injection overriding one citizen's system instructions (§4.2); spread: number of infected agents over turns follows logistic growth to full infection (§5.2, Fig. 6a); defense_family: LLM Tagging 'prepends a marker to agent responses, indicating that the message originates from another agent' plus marking/instruction defense (§6, Table 2); defense_evaluated_against: ASR of infection attacks under each defense (Fig. 7)
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending.

failure_observed: Injected semantic and coordination faults (hallucination, inexecutable plans, blind trust, message storms) propagate silently and can collapse task success, especially in linear workflows.
locus_detail: System prompts at initialization (role ambiguity, blind trust), agent outputs intercepted at agent-to-agent and tool boundaries, message routing layer, and user prompt at MAS entry (instruction faults)
evaluation: 15 fault types on MetaGPT (HumanEval, 164), Table-Critic (WikiTQ, 400), Camel (WebShop, 251); Robustness Score, occurrence rate, local and end-to-end success; GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3, GPT-5-mini as injector; GPT-5 LLM-as-judge for behavior labels (kappa 0.94)
limitation: Reviewer: three systems, two models, single-trial Pass@1 runs; faults are synthetic injections.
evidence_note: trigger: controlled fault injection via 'prompt modification, interception and response rewriting, and message routing manipulation' (§3.2), no adversary; trigger_evidence_level: only injected faults; locus: system and user prompt corruption, agent output rewriting, message routing (§3.2, §4.1.2)
review_note: adjudicated by Claude on the user's instruction, not by a human; human check pending.

evaluation: Who&When: failure logs from 127 MAS on GAIA and AssistantBench, 184 annotated failure tasks; agent-level and step-level accuracy; all-at-once, step-by-step, binary search; GPT-4o, GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1, Qwen-2.5, o1, DeepSeek R1

limitation: Best method reaches 53.5% agent-level and 14.2% step-level accuracy; long logs hard to annotate, Magentic-One GAIA subset limited to 30 instances.
evidence_note: trigger: logs of systems 'that fail to successfully address the queries' in normal benchmark runs (§3.1), no attacks; trigger_evidence_level: only benign failure logs; locus: decisive error (i, t) = agent i's mistaken action at step t (§2)

failure_observed: Communicating LLM agents can hide information in innocuous-looking messages (steganography) to collude or leak secrets without detection by an overseer.
locus_detail: Public channel between sender agent A and receiver agent B monitored by overseer E; insider-trading case: advisor agent's output to a malicious user sharing common knowledge
evaluation: Individual capability evals (Schelling points, ciphers, couplings, self-sampling) and group covertext steganography evals with overseer; coordination and undetected-decoding rates; GPT-2, Llama 2 7B/70B, Mixtral 8x7B, GPT-3.5, GPT-4
limitation: Current models' steganographic capabilities remain limited; most mitigations are analysed theoretically rather than tested.
evidence_note: trigger: sender prompted that 'An overseer... advantage you and the receiver have is a paragraph of common knowledge' to hide a secret (App. G.2), and insider case decoded 'by a malicious user' (App. I); emergent use without explicit instruction only qualitative; trigger_evidence_level: no benign-only condition tested quantitatively; locus: covert messages on 'a public channel accessible to overseer E' (App. G.2); defense_family: overseer monitoring tested in group evals, paraphrasing and parameter optimisation analysed by theorems (§7); defense_evaluated_against: overseer detection measured, 'evading detection by the overseer in 26% of the runs' (App. G.2), paraphrasing formal-only (Thm. 4)

evaluation: PI (CSQA, MMLU, GSM8K), TA (InjecAgent), MA (PoisonRAG); agent-level ASR and MDSR over 3 rounds; GPT-4o-mini and Qwen3-235B-A22B; chain, tree, star, random topologies; scaled to 20 and 50 agents; baselines G-Safeguard, AgentSafe, AgentXposed, Challenger, Inspector

failure_observed: A specification-compliant adversary exploits missing protocol primitives in A2A to inject into others' contexts, harvest credentials across delegation hops and exfiltrate data via unattested capability claims.
locus_detail: A2A protocol operations: client-supplied contextId without ownership check, multi-hop delegation chains losing identity, agent card skill claims without attestation
evaluation: 929 formalized statements, FSM of 37 states and 76 transitions; 11 vulnerabilities; 73.3% precision and 84.6% F1 vs manual review; zero-shot Claude Opus 4.6 baseline; PSMBench FSM extraction; Alloy and TLA+/TLC models
limitation: No running multi-agent system or executable exploit; mitigations formally verified for three findings only.
evidence_note: trigger: 'adversary... exploits gaps in the A2A protocol specification by sending protocol-conformant messages' (§3.2); trigger_evidence_level: only an adversary is modelled; locus: SendMessage with another client's contextId (§6), delegation chain, agent card claims (Table 2); defense_family: context ownership, verifiable delegation context, third-party skill attestation (§6 Mitigation); defense_evaluated_against: 'adding the proposed primitive restores the invariant' in Alloy and TLA+/TLC models, no experiment (§6 Formal Verification)
